newsitem.title: USA: U.S. confirms waiver for relief flight to Cuba.
newsitem.headline: U.S. confirms waiver for relief flight to Cuba.

text.p: The U.S. government has waived a ban on direct flights from the United States to Cuba to let a Roman Catholic Church charity send a planeload of aid for victims of Hurricane Lili, State Department officials said on Wednesday.

"A license was granted yesterday to Catholic Relief Services for a relief flight into Cuba," an official said, confirming a statement in Havana Tuesday by the Cuban Catholic organisation Caritas Cubana.
Caritas director Rolando Suarez said the plane would probably fly from Miami to the central city of Cienfuegos on Wednesday or Thursday with some 78 tons of food aid.
Suarez said it would be the first aid to arrive following an international appeal Monday by Caritas Cubana.

Hurricane Lili swept central and western areas of Cuba last Thursday and Friday. It destroyed more than 5,000 homes and damaged 78,000, as well as causing extensive damage to crops, power lines and communications.

The aid plane will be a rare direct flight from the United States since President Bill Clinton banned charter flights to and from the island after Cuba shot down two small private U.S. planes Feb. 24. Cuban athletes were allowed to fly directly to and from Atlanta in July for the Olympic Games.
The State Department official said the waiver had been granted because there was "clearly a need in Cuba" and because U.S. private citizens were anxious to help.

The official described the waiver as "completely consistent" with the Cuban Democracy Act and the Helms-Burton Act, which enforce sanctions against the communist-ruled island but also allow for waivers.

He said that since the Cuban Democracy Act was passed in 1992, the United States had sent about $140 million in aid to private groups in Cuba -- more than all private donations to Cuba from all sources in the world combined.
"The issue is how we ensure we are not giving aid to the Cuban government," said the official.

Cuban Americans, mostly in Florida, have mobilised to send aid to Cuba, but some say no aid should be sent to the island. They argue that such help might not reach victims of the storm but would be used by the government of President Fidel Castro.
